extracted.intended_audience: new and junior mathematics faculty (assistant professors) at universities
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for early-career mathematics faculty on duties including cooperative teaching, use of media, manuscript preparation, research expectations, committee service, mentoring, advising, professional society participation, and translation work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated management for large courses
rubrics_metrics.description: At a large state university ... it is common to put a Professor—usually one of the five who is giving the lectures—in charge of the whole course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five Professors should meet regularly to discuss issues connected with the course (management of the TAs; construction and scheduling of the exams; proctoring of the exams; grading issues (for both homework and exams); pacing of the course, order of topics, reaching of milestones on key dates; overall grading policies; coordination of office hours; coordination with the math lab). Such coordination requires management and oversight and can save labor for everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to a rigid common syllabus and lesson plan
rubrics_metrics.description: It is really best if the five lecturers stick to a rigid syllabus and lesson plan, so that on any given day they are all teaching the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all lectures follow the same plan then students who miss a class can attend another lecture without falling behind, and lecturers reach the same milestones enabling common midterms. This requires discipline but yields considerable payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide student flexibility across lecturers
rubrics_metrics.description: You can tell students that they are welcome at any professor’s office hour. ... Student can have a choice of several review sessions ... They can attend several different recitation sessions if they wish to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cross-attendance of office hours, review sessions, and recitations; it is well received by students and does not appreciably increase faculty workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common exams and coordinated grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically the five professors ... will have a common syllabus, give common exams, and coordinate their grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common exams and coordinated grading save labor, ensure consistency across sections, and help colleagues learn from each other; requires effort to arrange but beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat course coordination as collegial collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: You should of course expend every effort to get along with your colleagues ... to see their point of view, to work together to make everyone’s life easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the shared task congenial and productive; cooperation is in everyone's best interest and can improve course outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose presentation media appropriately and design slides effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages of overhead/opaque/projectors ... There are also several disadvantages ... There is a temptation to put too much material on each slide. You must learn to design slides effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider visibility, ability to preprepare graphics, portability and polish vs. lost intimacy, pacing difficulties, temptation to overload slides, and linear lock-in. Re-train pacing for slide-driven lectures and avoid overloading frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PowerPoint/Beamer judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: PowerPoint is quite a flexible and powerful tool. ... Some people are critical of PowerPoint ... It can be too slick, it can distance you from your audience, it can be superficial. ... Beamer ... has much of the functionality of PowerPoint ... but it also allows you to include any mathematics that can be rendered in TEX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PowerPoint/Beamer when appropriate; be aware of pros (color, video, animation, portability) and cons (distance from audience, superficiality). For mathematical content consider Beamer to render TEX accurately; still attend to frame design and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare manuscripts electronically (use TeX) and retain source files
rubrics_metrics.description: Most mathematicians prepare their own manuscripts—even book manuscripts—in TEX. Advantages: The author now has complete control over layout, content, and accuracy. The author retains the electronic *.tex and *.dvi files and can post them ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and archive TeX source and derivative PDFs, provide graphics via suitable tools (Adobe Illustrator, CorelDRAW, xfig), post preprints to arXiv, and submit papers by sending PDFs or arXiv pointers to journals. Electronic preparation gives control but requires new skills and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of disadvantages of electronic manuscript workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: There are also disadvantages to the new system. Some of these are: The mathematician is now required—for manuscript preparation—to learn skills (TEX, Adobe Illustrator, various operating system maneuvers) that used to be relegated to staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to learn TeX, graphics tools, operating system commands, spend substantial typing time, maintain an electronic profile, possibly learn HTML, and invest time in maintaining web infrastructure and document management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a professional personal web page and update regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: These days most of us have a personal Web page. That page commonly includes: a version of the CV; courses taught; professional affiliations; national committee service; conferences being organized; links to newsgroups and chat rooms; a list of publications and preprints; links to those publications and preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat your department web page as a business document. Ideally update the Web page once per week, update the online CV every few months, keep posted preprints and papers current. Recognize maintenance is time-consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize research expectations vary by institution
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are at a research university—what we ... call a Group I school—then research is supposed to be a big part of your life. ... At other schools, where there is a greater emphasis on teaching and service, the amount of time spent on research will be less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At research institutions allocate substantial time (possibly half of professional time) to research activities (reading, correspondence, thinking, conferences, grants, writing). For tenure you need a track record of scholarly publishing. In industry/government expect applied or constrained research, often not publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take committee service seriously and be prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: Take this work seriously. Show up punctually for meetings and be prepared. If there is reading material for a meeting, be sure to read it and understand it. Ask questions of someone if you don’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participate meaningfully, do background research when tasked, write reports when asked, and use committee work to learn about other departments and contribute positively. Avoid public criticism of colleagues; maintain professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit your committee load strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Many departments will reduce the service duties of a young (non-tenured) faculty member. ... Try to stay awake during committee meetings. ... It is important not to have too many committees, as who will serve on them? Nobody wants to be part of more than two or at most three committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a junior faculty member decline excessive service, serve on at most two or three departmental committees, and at most one or two university-wide committees per year; politely point out a full plate when asked to take on more.

rubrics_metrics.name: If chairing a committee, lead with preparation and a plan
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are [asked to chair a committee] then you should agree to do so and you should apply yourself to the task with aplomb and determination. Do the necessary background reading. Talk to people and find out the history ... Formulate a plan of action. Meet individually with the members of the committee and generate a working esprit de corps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify goals, prepare background, delegate, meet regularly, and build team cohesion so the committee accomplishes its tasks and leaves a positive impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage constructively at faculty meetings and understand governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A faculty meeting is a gathering of equals. ... The primary vehicle for decision-making at faculty meetings is discussion. ... Some decisions ... can be made by consensus. Others will take a show of hands. The really delicate ones are handled by secret ballot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participate in discussion, respect differing voices and governance structures (Chair vs Head), know voting options (consensus, show of hands, secret ballot), and use meetings to inform and focus on departmental matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor with patience, fairness, confidentiality, and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mentoring requires patience, perspective, fairness, and sound judgment. Many people will take a mentoring transaction as an opportunity to criticize and rat out their colleagues. This is tempting, but a dreadfully bad idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace mentoring opportunities, answer typical mentee questions (organizing classes, writing exams, grading, managing TAs, jump-starting research, choosing journals/grants/conferences), avoid airing colleagues' faults, and provide supportive guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise undergraduates knowledgeably and diplomatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of your job as a Math Professor is to be an advisor or counselor to some undergraduates. ... Often advising consists in just reading the University or College Catalog a little more patiently and a little more carefully than the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know breadth requirements, prerequisites, course flavors; be diplomatic when advising about instructors; refer policy or substitution questions to the Vice-Chair for Undergraduate Studies; refer students with serious personal problems to professional counselors; supervise and edit honors theses carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support graduate students and dissertation candidates appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes students who are struggling with the quals seek advice. ... I have had graduate students ... seek out advice because they were having personal or financial difficulties ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide study and time-management advice for quals, point students to Vice-Chair when appropriate, offer guidance for students facing difficulties, serve as faculty mentor for oral presentations, and be mindful that dissertation advising has additional expectations (see chapter sections referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in and support professional societies
rubrics_metrics.description: I feel strongly that you, a budding mathematician, should belong to one or more of these professional societies. Membership is relatively inexpensive ... And the benefits are considerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join societies (AMS, MAA, SIAM, AWM, NAM, SACNAS, etc.) to access conferences, journals, networking, and professional tools; recognize societies' role in sustaining the profession and aiding career development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide or assist with high-quality translations; avoid relying on machine translators for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: One important service that a mathematician can provide to the profession is as a translator. ... There are automatic Online translators—Google has one—that one can use for free ... These tools do not work very well, and they are particularly poor with technical languages like mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer human translation assistance (particularly for Russian and Chinese texts historically) when possible; do not depend on machine translation for technical mathematical content; recognize English predominance but value accurate translation work.
